title: Strat Chat - Document Cameras/Visualisers
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, a public school leader, explains how he finally made a document camera (visualiser) work in his lessons after owning one for a year without using it. The breakthrough, learned from Dr Nathaniel Swain at researchED Melbourne, was embedding the camera feed into a PowerPoint deck with the Cameo feature so he can switch between slides and live modelling without clunky transitions. His rationale is cognitive load: a visualiser shows modelled writing in the same form as students' own work, so they spend no working memory translating between the two, and they see the physical motion of composition. He describes four uses with senior classes during exam revision: breaking down a case study with annotations, live modelled responses, showcasing student work as exemplars, and projecting the same worksheet with sentence stems for students to expand. He reports more active engagement, especially when he adds frequent opportunities to respond. The post also gives brief set-up steps and a note on a budget camera.
points: The key practical insight is to embed the document camera in PowerPoint through Insert Cameo and Camera Format, which removes the transition friction that had stopped regular use.
A visualiser reduces cognitive load because the modelled text matches students' own page, so working memory is spent on the thinking rather than on transferring it.
Seeing the physical motion of writing being modelled matters for composition, and typed or animated slides cannot provide it.
Four concrete uses are offered: case study breakdowns, live modelled responses, showcasing student exemplars after checking for understanding, and sentence stems on the same projected worksheet.
Brien moves from 'I do' to 'We do' co-construction and pairs the tool with many chances for students to respond, which he says keeps the modelling from being passive.
quotes: A document camera/visualiser is a tool to display modelled writing and exemplar responses in a way that exactly matches the students’ work. This helps to optimise cognitive load as students do not need to use any additional resources in working memory to transfer what you’re doing, to what they’re doing.

First, they were never physically seeing the motion of writing being modelled which is an important part of the composition and secondly, it was a passive experience for the students and I had no way of really know if they were actively thinking throughout my modelling.

It wasn’t until I saw Dr Nathaniel Swain presenting at researchED in Melbourne in August of 2026 that my mind was able to be casually blown by the simplicity of the reveal that you can embed your document camera into your slide deck in PowerPoint to seamlessly switch between modes of teaching.
One of my pet peeves with many of my students is that they do not spend the time with a large body of text in an assessment and annotate it to build the meaning in how it relates to the curriculum.

After completing a check for understanding and circulating the room being able to highlight a student response and provide positive and constructive feedback on the response as a class can be a powerful tool for filling in any gaps which may exist in some segments of the class.

Another tool I have found useful is whenever students have a worksheet or practice exam to have the exact same sheet projected on the board and provide sentence stems or fragments/kernels for students to then expand upon to lessen the cognitive load of options related to beginning the task.

Anecdotally I have noticed that students are far more actively engaged in the modelled response using this tool, especially as I have been practicing including more opportunities to respond throughout the use.
